questions.question: Draw an electron density map for a molecule of oxygen (O2).
questions.answer: Symmetrical map with highest electron density between the two O nuclei (the double bond region), falling away from the nuclei.
steps: Each O atom has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more for a full octet.
Two O atoms share two pairs of electrons, forming a double bond (O=O).
Electron density is highest in the region between the two nuclei, where the shared pairs sit.
The map is symmetrical about the midpoint of the bond and falls off away from the nuclei.

questions.question: Draw a diagram to show the shape of a water (H2O) molecule and give its bond angle.
questions.answer: Bent (V-shaped) with an H-O-H bond angle of 104.5 deg, with two lone pairs on O shown.
steps: O has 6 outer electrons; 2 form O-H bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs.
There are 4 electron pairs around O, arranged tetrahedrally.
Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs give a bent (V-shaped) molecule.
Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so the bond angle is reduced from 109.5 deg to 104.5 deg.

questions.question: Complete the dot-and-cross diagram for POCl3 (crosses for P electrons, dots for Cl electrons, circles for O electrons).

questions.question: Explain the shape of the POCl3 molecule using electron-pair repulsion theory.
questions.answer: Tetrahedral around P with bond angles of about 109.5 deg (no lone pairs on P).
steps: P has four regions of electron density: the P=O double bond counts as one region, plus three P-Cl bonds.

questions.question: Explain how the electrical conductivity, high melting temperature and malleability of metals depend on their structure and bonding.
questions.answer: Conductivity: delocalised electrons move and carry charge. High melting point: strong electrostatic attraction between cations and electrons is hard to overcome. Malleability: layers of cations slide without breaking the bonding.
steps: Electrical conductivity: delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge when a voltage is applied.
High melting temperature: the strong electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalised electrons needs a lot of energy to overcome.
Malleability: layers of cations can slide over each other because the electron sea keeps attracting the ions, so bonds are not broken.
Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the structure deforms without fracturing.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the physical properties of diamond and graphite differ, referring to structure and bonding.
questions.answer: (1) Diamond is very hard, graphite is soft and slippery. (2) Graphite conducts electricity, diamond does not.
steps: Diamond: each C bonds to 4 others in a giant tetrahedral covalent lattice, so it is very hard with a high melting temperature.
Graphite: each C bonds to 3 others in hexagonal layers; the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide and it is soft.
Graphite: each C has one spare electron that is delocalised over the layers, so graphite conducts electricity.
Diamond: all four outer electrons are used in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons and it does not conduct.

questions.question: State how the structure of graphene is related to the structure of graphite.
questions.answer: Graphene is a single layer (one sheet) of the hexagonal carbon structure of graphite.
steps: Graphite consists of many layers of hexagonal carbon rings held together by weak forces.
Graphene is one of these layers, a single sheet of carbon atoms one atom thick.
So graphene is a single layer of graphite.

questions.question: State a use for graphene and identify the property that makes it suitable for that use.
questions.answer: Use: conducting material in electronic devices (e.g. electrodes or touch screens). Property: high electrical conductivity from delocalised electrons. Any valid use linked to this property is accepted.
steps: Each graphene sheet has delocalised electrons across its structure.
These electrons are free to move, so graphene conducts electricity very well.
Use: as a conductor in electronic devices, such as electrodes or touch screens.
Property: high electrical conductivity, which makes it suitable for this use.

questions.question: State what is meant by metallic bonding.
questions.answer: The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions (cations) and delocalised electrons.
steps: Metal atoms lose outer electrons to form a lattice of positive ions.
The outer electrons are delocalised and move freely through the lattice.
The electrostatic attraction between the cations and this sea of electrons is metallic bonding.

questions.question: Explain why metallic bonding in magnesium is much stronger than in sodium.
questions.answer: Mg atoms contribute 2 delocalised electrons (Na contributes 1), and Mg2+ is smaller and more highly charged than Na+, giving stronger electrostatic attraction.
steps: Each Mg atom contributes 2 delocalised electrons; each Na atom contributes 1.
More delocalised electrons give a greater charge density in the electron sea.
Mg2+ is smaller and has a 2+ charge, so its charge density is higher than that of Na+.
The stronger electrostatic attraction needs more energy to break, giving a higher melting temperature.

questions.question: Describe the attraction between the atoms in a covalent bond.
questions.answer: Electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the positive nuclei of both atoms.
steps: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
The shared pair is negatively charged and is attracted to the positive nuclei of both atoms.
This electrostatic attraction holds the atoms together.

questions.question: Explain why silicon has a much higher melting temperature than phosphorus, by referring to their structures.
questions.answer: Silicon is a giant covalent lattice, so strong covalent bonds must be broken. Phosphorus is simple molecular, so only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome.
steps: Silicon has a giant covalent lattice in which each atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds.
Melting silicon requires breaking these strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice, which needs a lot of energy.
Phosphorus has simple molecules (P4) held in a lattice by weak van der Waals forces.
Melting phosphorus only overcomes these weak intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds, so less energy is needed.
